questions.lead_in: What type of outbreak is represented in the epidemic curve?
questions.explanation: Propagated progressive source An epidemic curve is a visual display of the onset of illness during an outbreak. Point source epidemics involve a common source and occur over a brief period. Common persistent courses rise and fall, but the cases do not occur within a single incubation period. Intermittent outbreaks are separated by periods without evidence of infection.

a) A healthcare-associated outbreak is an increase in the number of cases of an infection/colonization (or a specific organism) above the number normally expected (baseline rate) in a defined population, over a defined time period, within a healthcare facility or unit, that is epidemiologically linked.

questions.model_answer: a) Two immediate actions: (1) Notify infection prevention and control/public health and the laboratory director immediately (possible Bacillus anthracis, a Tier 1 select agent/bioterrorism concern). (2) Handle the specimen within a biosafety cabinet using BSL-2/3 precautions, halt further routine bench workup, and refer to a reference/public health laboratory (Laboratory Response Network) for confirmatory testing. b) Three tests to identify the organism: (1) Lysis by gamma phage (specific for B. anthracis). Infection control measures for lab technician.

What are 2-indications to treat?

cohort_answer.text: Nurse: Routine practices. Lab technician: Laboratory Safety and Containment - infective stage (conidia) present in sporulating mold form cultures and soil from endemic areas; yeast form in tissues/fluids may cause local infection via parenteral inoculation or mucous membrane splash; BSL-2/ABSL-2 practices recommended for handling/processing clinical specimens, identifying isolates, animal tissues, mold cultures (any culture identifying dimorphic fungi handled in Class II BSC); BSL-3 practices for propagating sporulating cultures in mold form or processing soil/environmental materials likely to contain infectious conidia. questions.question: Two patients in your hospital have acquired Legionella pneumonia. The source is suspected to be the potable water distribution system in your hospital.

parts.text: What are TWO short-term solutions that can be implemented to immediately reduce the risk of infection?
What are THREE long-term solutions to prevent the risk of infection in the future?

questions.model_answer:
a) Two short-term solutions to immediately reduce risk from a contaminated potable water system: (1) Superheat-and-flush of the hot water system (raise water temperature to ≥70°C/158°F and flush all outlets/taps). (2) Hyperchlorination of the water system, and/or temporary installation of point-of-use filters on faucets and showerheads in high-risk patient care areas.
b) Three long-term solutions: (1) Implementation of a formal water management program (e.g., per ASHRAE 188) with regular risk assessment and monitoring for Legionella. (2) Installation of a supplemental disinfection system, such as copper-silver ionization or chlorine dioxide/monochloramine treatment of the water supply. (3) Engineering modifications to the plumbing system (e.g., eliminating dead legs/areas of water stagnation, optimizing hot water temperature control) to reduce ongoing colonization risk.
